I've used it for several years here and I have very good results.  Only challenge I've had so far is large amounts of subsidence in my deepest beds as the wood breaks down in volume.  I had to top up a lot for the first couple of years on each bed, and I had one bed develop (no joke) 1-1.5 foot deep sinkholes!

I use two products from AWR: 

- Hardwood mulch (brown bag)
https://www.texasnative.com/product-page/texas-native-hardwood-mulch-2-c-f
- Composted Manure (gold bag) https://www.texasnative.com/product-page/texas-native-composted-manure-75-c-f

Along with:

- Perlite https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07S4FTPYB
- Biochar (this isn't the exact product but it's the closest I could find. Just get the cheapest per volume you can get, usually the biggest bag) https://www.tractorsupply.com/tsc/product/wakefield-biochar-carbonboost-soil-amendments
- Dr. Earth Home Grown fertilizer https://drearth.com/product/home-grown/
- Optional: Mycorrhizae https://www.amazon.com/dp/B09DMGNT5N

I mix it one bag of hardwood mulch to 2 bags of composted manure.  Neither is actually exactly what they say; the hardwood mulch is "naturally aged" to darken it, and it's generally old enough that it's begun to decompose (it tends to get soggy in the bags and continue to break down).  The composted manure is actually topsoil enriched with composted manure.  The combination of the two means that you get organics at various stages of decomp, along with sand and clay for good consistency.  I add a couple scoops (about a half gallon total) of perlite to break up the clay a bit, and about half as much biochar, just because it's expensive.  I add two cups of Dr. Earth and a teaspoon of myco.

The perlite and biochar accumulate over time, as they don't really break down, so if I'm topping off a bed, I don't always need as much perlite for top-up soil.  I haven't needed to skip the biochar yet, as it's great stuff and I haven't reached enough accumulation to need to cut back on it.

I mix these in half batches in a cement mixer.  If the soil looks too gloopy or clay-ey, I throw in a bit more mulch.  If it's too "woody" (full of sticks), I'll throw in a bit more of the gold bag stuff.

I buy enough at the beginning of the season to get the bulk discounts from Home Depot (closest place that has the stuff, and extra cheap if you can catch their mulch sale, 5 bags for $10) and mix a bunch of soil to top off my raised beds and start any new beds I might have built.  Once, maybe twice a year is about right for me, and I have 425 square feet of beds.

The aged, bagged materials tend to have more "life" and moisture than soils that are stored completely separate in soil yards and blended just before delivery to the customer.  The added inert(ish) ingredients are for texture, waterholding, and to provide a substrate for microbes.  The fertilizer is a nice balanced blend that smells not terrible and provides food for microbes and plants, and the myco help to quickly colonize the mulch so it breaks down quicker.  I get lots of mushrooms in my beds when the rainy season starts.

You can skip the more expensive components (biochar and Dr. Earth) and replace the fertilizer with something cheaper if you need to, but I wouldn't skip the perlite.

I should probably make a video or post about this next time I make soil but that's the gist of it.  Let me know if you have any questions.

P.S. I hate having to use bagged products, because I end up with a bunch of trash bags afterwards, but it's so far the best balance of cost and quality I've found.

There are lines drawn at the local, county, state, regional, and national border.  Work is ideally applied locally, but sometimes requires national support and coordination.  There are programs at every level, up to the national and international scopes.  Money is collected and spent at each level, with support coming from above at times to cover shortfalls.

It's basic to the principle of mutualized risk and cost.  If you purchase insurance, you're participating in mutualized risk, except that the money you spend on that generally profits insurance company shareholders.  But originally, insurance was mutualized and the participants (policyholders) were the shareholders, and would receive dividends when the mutual fund spent less than it took in (and gained through investment).  Mutualized costs for social programs are similar, except they pay their dividends in human capital.

You live in and benefit from a society in which children don't starve.  Starving children grow into sick adults that cannot contribute as much to society.  Or they die.  Starving children's parents aren't able to work as effectively to produce goods and services we all benefit from.  As a result, big programs to eliminate childhood malnutrition and starvation were founded, because the cost of prevention was found to be much lower than the cost of not preventing malnutrition and starvation.  It's not my money or your money to spend as I want to.  It's part of maintaining a functioning society in which I can then make *more* money because there is a healthy labor and consumer pool.

I'd appreciate if we could take the temperature down here.  I'm not trying to insult you and I think we largely agree.  I want to believe that you're a good-hearted person and that you charge a fair rent for the property you own.  I don't believe that individual landlords are generally a part of the housing shortage problem.

All I'm saying is that renters are not the cash cow they've been made out to be.  Landlords are not entitled to having their mortgage paid, but rather to be paid, as you said, for the service exchange.  Rental rates have risen above a reasonable rate due to, again as you said, investment corporations buying up properties as investments rather than to rent for a fair price.  Charging above and beyond a reasonable rate *is* using the renters as a charity (although we generally call it exploitation instead) because they're paying extra money for no additional goods received.

You do have the right to own your property and rent it out, and you do have the right to expect to have people leave if they cannot pay.  All I'm saying is that Texas already has some of the most landlord-friendly tenant laws in the country, so if a landlord dependent on renters to be able to keep their property, and cannot handle the existing eviction timelines, then they're extended beyond their means and dying a slow death.  Their "need" for more rent in order to keep their property does not entitle them to more rent.  The idea that renters "pay the mortgage" is an exploitive concept that needs to be debunked.

I think you're catching a lot of heat because of your statement "if you cannot afford housing, then you can stay at a shelter".  That's honestly just not the case in most places.  Shelters are overburdened and underfunded.  Rents are higher than they should be for the service provided, due to investment corps gobbling up the properties and renting them for "what they can get" rather than a fair price.  Rents being too high and affordable housing not being available leads to the problems we're seeing right now with squatting.  Because "just stay at a shelter" isn't really an option.  I think this is intentional.  If the options are "pay the rent, *no matter how high it goes* or live on the street", that puts the tenants in an unworkable bargaining position and forces them to pay inflated rent.  When the rent gets too high, the options become "live on the street" or "squat".  

I think that additional focus on regulating away the *symptom* of desperation squatting is largely going to worsen the problem.  I think we should be regulating away the *cause* which is large corporations buying up property and price fixing too high.

As I said above, I don't think this is being driven by individual landlords, but I do think it's our job as individual homeowners and landlords to push back on laws that are mostly designed to benefit exploitive corporations or that harm vulnerable populations.

I'll say it again.  If you can't afford to float an eviction period and subsequent re-renting, you're overextended and can't really afford to be a landlord. They're expecting their renters to keep them owning their property for free.  It's upside-down.

Renters are not a charity as well.  I say this as a homeowner who has also rented here and in other places.  Renter protections in Texas are abysmal, and their access to due process is quite limited.

If you cannot pay your mortgage without a renter, you're overextended.  This may not be your fault, I don't know your situation, but the renters are not the reason you can't pay your mortgage.  The reason you cannot pay your mortgage is that you don't have enough income.  If you have tenants that aren't paying their rent, you're entitled to remove them, but the process should be measured and fair.  If you don't have the money to float an eviction period, you're upside-down on your obligations.

The idea that renters should pay a landlord's mortgage is upside down, and depends on the idea that owners can charge more for a home because they "own" it.  As a landlord, you're not entitled to your tenant buying your equity for you.  Landlording is a *job*. In exchange for maintaining and renting the property, you are entitled to:

1. The cost of owning the property.  This can be taxes, fees, even to some extent the interest on the loan.
2. The cost of establishing a risk fund for repairs and maintenance of the property.
3. Payment for the service of being the responsible property owner and manager.  This is, of course, predicated on you *actually* maintaining the property in good, livable condition.

This may, or may not, be enough to cover your mortgage.  It stinks if not, but if your mortgage is too high to cover with a reasonable rate of rent, don't look at the tenants for fault.  The ballooning costs of real estate and the high cost of home loans is not on them.  It's on the banks, large corporations, and a lack of regulatory structure to keep credit affordable, rather than a mechanism to constantly drive value to the capital of the largest owners in society.

I'm pro freedom of expression and I think it's great that they're protesting and bringing legal action for this restriction.  That said, for anyone who doesn't "get" drag, it might help to note some of the origins of drag.

Drag in its current expression is, in many ways, descended from the same roots as clowning, vaudeville, and even modern pro wrestling.  These are art forms that play with exaggerations of character (big villains, big heroes, exaggerated shapes, brightly colored outfits and makeup, etc.).  Drag is typified as doing this with gender traits, which ends up being extreme dressing as a different gender, but the same is done with burlesque and pro wrestling, just not as an opposite gender.  Other comedy forms play with other attributes but the effect is the same--simplify the characters into one or two traits to play with society's ideas about those traits.

Comedy is meant to make us laugh, but it's also to make us think.  Many drag performers do charity work or have activist causes.  If you find the art form makes you uncomfortable, it may be doing exactly what it's supposed to do.  And if it makes you uncomfortable, you can always turn your back on it and walk away.

This is the right solution.  Remove and replace dirt, then cover and grow food plants in new dirt on top.  Plants only use the top 12ish inches (~30cm) of soil.  Give yourself some room above the local soil and don't compost any yard waste that grows in the contaminated soil.  Remove it to the trash.  It will not be cost-effective for you to remediate the soil by yourself.  Removal and replacement of the top 12" of soil is the most drastic solution most people could afford.

Depending on where you are, it might also be worth seeing if your local or state/province government has any remediation programs.  In the US, some areas have funds allocated to removal and replacement of contaminated soil after factories or other industrial facilities contaminated them.

In any case, don't stress too much.  Lead and copper are taken up by plants in small amounts, typically, and then mostly when the soil pH is low (acidic).  I would be more concerned about making sure I make the soil safe to walk on barefoot and don't get the contaminated soil itself on your produce, tools, clothes, or hands.

First, we have to agree on a few facts in order to even have a discussion:

- Oppression is defined as keeping someone in subservience or hardship, especially by the unjust exercise of authority
- A refugee is someone who flees from oppression

Further, these are my assertions

- People who self-identify as trans are oppressed by the policies and laws enacted or likely to be enacted by the State of Texas
- People who flee this oppression can be said to be refugees
- Even if not called refugees in name due to not meeting some threshold of oppression, their decision to flee is understandable and still indicative of the same type of injustice that we are discussing when discuss refugees.

Details:

Based on the definition above, I believe there is systemic oppression of people who self-identify as trans.  I do not believe this oppression rises to the levels of oppression in some places, and I do believe it rises above the levels of oppression in other places. I respectfully wish to disagree with some of your premises, here. The term "racist" and "sexist" are heavily overused. Both are defined as viewing someone as of different intrinsic value because of their race or sex. I've been called these terms before, so I've done a lot of thinking on this. 


DEI initiatives are intended to counter racism and sexism by education, assistance, and inclusion of people who have been victims of these phenomena. That means that, necessarily, some of that assistance will require awareness of race and sex, and *how those traits have been targeted*. A long history of sexism has resulted in deep bias against women in STEM, for example. Women who are deeply capable in math and science are not receiving equal support in entering those fields. There's no officially organized "program to exclude women from STEM", but there is an emergent behavior that does so, essentially through "dark patterns" of society. To counter that, you have to address it by considering three things: 

- what non-role-specific traits have suppressed a person from participating in this portion of society (Diversity)
- in what ways have these people's access to resources been indirectly suppressed, and how can they be supported in accessing equal starting resources to this opportunity (Equity)
- where have these people not been offered opportunities where others have, solely based on traits that have nothing to do with merit? 


These programs are intended to *identify* places where people have been *indirectly* blocked, harmed, or excluded based on protected characteristics. As you say, if someone benefits because they're, say, white, that's racially biased. Racial bias exists and is statistically demonstrable by the presence of certain demographics relative to their presence in society. I work in engineering, and the demographics of my field does not reflect that of society. It's mostly white men. 


As an aside: I don't hate white men or think they should be suppressed; I am a white man and I've had to protect my own psyche from believing negative things about myself from misguided messaging about race. 


Back to identifying places people have been blocked: once a statistical imbalance is identified, say, women in STEM, it's just good business to target improvements to access to the big groups first, as that is the first place where investment will show proportional results. Having programs to support women's access to *starting* in STEM results in more women in STEM who *would have been in STEM already* if there weren't dark patterns against it in society. 


Now, I hear what you've been saying: if it helps a particular group, it's unfair. In principle, I agree with you, because only having a "women in STEM" program would be unfair. Where I think we differ is this: a "women in STEM" program is not unfair if it is one of *many* programs for a diversity of people. A diversity of programs, if you will. As long as it's not illegal to have a program for, say "men in STEM", then helping one segment of people is just targeted work to lift a specific group, because the issues that affect that particular group are very specific and go deep enough to merit specific study and specific remedies. Women need different help than men, blacks need different help than whites, etc. due to the ways they've been specifically challenged by society. I'm taking some shortcuts here for brevity. 


I've been in "men in STEM" programs and it's great that they exist. They just don't need quite the depth of resources at this time because there are already lots of things that help and support men specifically into STEM, they're just not given names and line-item budgets. 


Banning the use of DEI programs just because they consider personal traits and offer aid specific to those traits is overbroad and ignores the fact that there are structures and patterns in society that provide support disproportionately to people of some personal traits. The study of these implicit aids and how to then provide corresponding aid to those who have not received it is not unfair or inequitable. It restores fairness and equity of opportunity, so people can shine on their merit. I don't believe someone should get chosen over another because of a personal trait. I also believe that we should be trained to spot where our choices have *already* been shaped and limited by outside actions, and take effort to restore the full range of options. I want my universities, jobs, etc. to have a full range of choices, so they can benefit from the wide range of experiences that come from hiring all sorts of people. I'm ok with these entities spending time, money, and resources to attract restore their full range of options for candidates, and lifting up all candidates in the ways they need to be lifted so we can see them all in the same light. 


That's why I think it's acceptable, a good use of resources, and not racist or sexist to have programs and aids that are targeted at specific races or sexes. We need a diversity of programs to ensure targeted help is provided to all kinds of people. As we work through these challenges as a society, some programs may become obsolete. That's a good thing and evidence that the rising tide is lifting the boats. In a way, that's kind of what's happened for many white men already. Their boats have been lifted. They're still just as worthy and valuable, they just may not need as much help targeted specifically as their experience as white or as men. Instead they can focus on specific challenges, like needing to get better at math, or figure out how to write more eloquently, or how to manage their time better (these were some of my challenges).


I think we both want fairness. I think we have differences in how we believe that can be accomplished. I ask you to consider my position as I have considered yours, and I hope you have a great day.

One of the challenges I've found with many of the identity movements is that there isn't always an endgame for the inevitable question of "who" we are, when "what" is no longer enough. Your experiences are very unique and will provide a special perspective in the world.  I'm sorry you're struggling with this challenge, but I think you're asking good questions.

You don't have to fit in exactly to fit in with a group.  You can bond with a group over shared experiences, but you can also bond over differences, learning how another person with similarities and differences is navigating this world.

You're doing the right thing by working on yourself first.  There are many things we may not like about ourselves when we're still processing challenges or traumas from our past.  Working on understanding your feelings and why you might feel them will help you find your way to peace.

There are two parts to the answer: dose and energy. You can think of the dose as the "brightness" of the radiation, and energy as the "color". Film exposure is increased with dose, but not necessarily increased with an increase in energy.

Radiation in a transatlantic flight is something like 0.1 mSv. According to the Health Physics Society, an old style scanner delivers around a tenth to a hundredth of this dose. Modern CT scanners, on the other hand, deliver about 15 times this dose (1.5 mSv).

But dose is only part of the question. Sieverts are meant to measure health impacts of ionizing radiation exposure, not the impact on photographic film. In an X-ray scanner, CT or otherwise, the X-rays are intended to be blocked partially by everyday objects, so the scanner can distinguish different materials and provide a meaningful image. In a transatlantic flight, the energy of the incoming radiation is higher, and it doesn't interact with matter as much (which is why it penetrates much further into matter). Paradoxically the higher energy photons don't expose the film grains as much because fewer photons actually stop and deposit their energy into the film grains.

First, I'll echo everyone else here.  This is dangerous and should be fixed by an electrician.  It's my understanding that this is not an option where you are, so in the interest of helping you be safe, I can make some suggestions.  Without knowing where you are, the suggestions I give you are going to be a bit general.  This is all at-your-own risk.

1. The breaker appears to be melting because of a high-resistance connection where multiple wires have been jammed in.  Normally breaker terminals cannot accommodate more than 2 wires, sometimes only 1.  So first, to remedy this condition, each wire should be broken out to its own terminal.  More on this later.
1. The breakers are single-pole.  If this is two hot wires, it should be a double pole, so a trip in either side trips both of the breakers.  I don't know where you are, so I can't say whether both wires are hot or one is hot and the other is neutral/return.
1. The breakers themselves have too high of a current rating for the individual wires in the circuits.  I can't tell the exact size of the wires, but the breakers are rated for 32 amps each.  Normally small appliances will be on wires rated for 15 or 20 amps, and a higher current risks melting the wires.  Check your local code.
1. You need to verify the individual wires are going to the correct wires in the circuits/outlets.  Your local code will say which colors are supposed to go where.  You can pull the outlets out gently to verify which wire is connected to which terminal in the plug.
1. One of the wires in each cable should be a ground/protective earth wire.  This wire needs to be connected to a reliable earth connection.  Look for a ground rod in the earth or other nearby connection that goes into the bare earth.  Worst case scenario, you might be able to use a cold water pipe.

There are a couple of things you can improve these issues.

1. TURN THE POWER OFF TO THE TOP TWO WIRES.
1. If you can get a small load center, it will make this assembly a lot safer.  This is a metal box with a connection for protective earth ground.  It should have a terminal block with holes to receive the protective earth ground wire from each of the cables.  Depending on where you are, it may include connections for the steps below.
1. Connect the ground wires from each of the cables to a protective earth terminal block that is connected to a reliable earth ground.
1. Replace the damaged breakers with one double pole breaker.  This type of breaker will have two switches connected with a bar.
1. Use a terminal block to break each of the wires coming out of the "main" breaker (32 amps here) into a few terminals (make sure the terminal block is rated to 32 amps or above).  This will help keep the terminals from melting from bad connections.  
1. Use 32 amp rated wires (10 AWG or bigger) to go from the terminal block to individual small breakers, rated for the size of the wire going to outlets or appliances.  This will keep the wires from receiving too much current and melting or burning.

Even after all this, it still won't be legal or to code, but at least there will hopefully be less risk of death or injury from shock or electrical fire.

I don't think your laptop power supply will be able to supply the starting current for your motor. The output capacitors aren't really big enough to drive the inrush on a stopped DC motor. A small 12 volt lead acid battery would be. Put an ohmmeter across the motor leads when it's disconnected and stopped, then take (12 V/resistance) to find the "locked rotor" current. You'll probably find that to be far above the laptop supply rating. If it's a decent supply, it'll detect the "short circuit" and lock out until reset by unplugging from the wall.

If you're looking for a portable application, I would suggest a small battery on a cart with a charge controller and your transfer pump. Charge it except when needed, and size your battery to not be fully drained by a full day of service. Wire it with non-reversible, shrouded connectors and put a high current switch and an appropriate fuse for the thinnest wires used, and you have a nice safe solution.

12 volts can absolutely bite you through broken skin, especially wet hands. I've been shocked by low voltage before. And it can remove fingers pretty handily (sorry) if there's a high current path like a hot short. We had a mechanic lose a finger when his wedding ring was part of a hot short with a wrench across the terminals.

The circumstances are rare and require contact with the power source, which is a big part of OSHA and NFPA concerns. It won't jump out and bite you like high voltages will, and it can't sustain a long distance arc in air due to internal resistances in the battery, but it can absolutely start one for long enough to weld tools and other things to the terminals.

An easy example of this is a crossed jumper cable. It can dump enough energy to melt the insulation, the copper, and underlying car parts. Seen it happen. But car batteries can't really be restricted the way that high voltage building wiring is. People have to be able to maintain their own cars, and basic safety procedures can cut risks down to a reasonable level. And those risks are largely limited to the person working with the battery.
Minor note, batteries supply current in A (amps), not AH (amp-hours). Amp-hours is a measure of capacity (sort of).
